questions.q: What does a merge field like {!Shift.ServiceResource} do inside an Email Template?
options: It blocks the email from sending until the field is filled in
It pulls live data from the record that triggered the notification into the email
It creates a new custom field on the Shift object
It converts the template into a validation rule
questions.explain: Merge fields pull real values from the triggering record, which is what makes one template reusable and specific instead of generic.

questions.q: Which tool blocks a record from being saved outright when data doesn't meet a standard?
options: Email Alerts
Validation Rules
Approval Processes
Reports
questions.explain: Validation Rules evaluate a formula and block the save, with an error message, when the formula returns true.

questions.q: In the Insert Field picker, what does a ">" after an object name like "Account >" indicate?
options: That field is required
That field is a formula field itself
The object has more related fields available if you drill in
The formula has a syntax error
questions.explain: The ">" marker means there are more fields nested under that relationship, letting a formula reach across to a related object.

questions.q: What does an Approval Step's Step Criteria control?
options: Whether all records reaching the step enter it, or only ones matching a condition
Which users can view the approval process definition
How many email templates the step can use
The object the approval process is defined on
questions.explain: Step Criteria lets a step be conditional, for example only discounts over 20% continue to a VP step, which is what makes multi-step routing possible.

questions.q: What appears on a record once its approval process is active and a user wants to start it?
options: A Delete button
A Clone button
A Submit for Approval action
A Change Owner action
questions.explain: Submit for Approval is the action that locks the record and sends it into the process, notifying the first step's approver.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the risk of treating "clicks before code" as an absolute rule?
options: It has no risk; it should always be followed without exception
It can lead to either an unreadable tangle of Flow elements, or reaching for Apex out of habit when declarative would do
It means validation rules can never be used
It requires every process to use Apex instead
questions.explain: Both failure modes are real: forcing complexity into Flow past the point of readability, or using Apex by habit when a simpler declarative tool would have worked.

questions.q: What is an automation "collision," as this lesson defines it?
options: A Salesforce error that always prevents a save
Two or more pieces of automation acting on the same save in an order the admin didn't fully anticipate, producing unexpected behavior
A validation rule with a syntax error
Any time two approval processes exist in the same org
questions.explain: A collision isn't one broken component, it's the unmapped interaction between multiple automations touching the same save.

questions.q: What happens if a duplicate rule blocks a record during the save procedure?
options: The record saves anyway with a warning
Only the validation rules are skipped, everything else still runs
The record isn't saved, and no further steps like after triggers or workflow rules run
The record is saved but marked inactive
questions.explain: A duplicate rule set to block stops the save procedure entirely at that point; after triggers and workflow never get a chance to run.

questions.q: What does the Description field on a validation rule or approval process ideally capture?
options: A restatement of the formula itself
The business reason it exists, any non-obvious edge case, and what would break if it were removed
The name of the Salesforce release it was created in
A list of every user who can view the object
questions.explain: The formula already shows what the rule checks. The Description should capture the why, which is what's lost when someone else has to maintain it later.

questions.q: What tool confirms exactly which criteria evaluated true or false for a specific test record?
options: Debug logs
The company's annual report
A manually maintained spreadsheet
The Salesforce mobile app's notification center
questions.explain: Debug logs show the actual evaluated logic for a given record, which is how a boundary case gets confirmed rather than assumed.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue the Chapter 3 method applies beyond the fictional case studies used to teach it?
options: Because the method only works for discount approvals specifically
Because fictional companies require a different method than real ones
The method does not apply outside of this course's exercises
Because the method doesn't change when the company and complaint are real instead of fictional
questions.explain: Complaint, requirements, design, documentation, and testing describe ordinary day-to-day administrator work, not a special advanced case.

questions.q: Why does a 12% discount never reach the Sales Director's approval queue?
options: The Sales Director opted out of the process
The two-step design routes it to the owner's manager instead, reserving the director for discounts over 25%
12% discounts are automatically rejected
Discounts under 15% skip approval entirely
questions.explain: Tiering approvers by severity means only deals large enough to justify senior attention reach the second step.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue documentation matters even for automation that's working correctly today?
options: Working automation never actually needs maintenance
Salesforce requires documentation to pass validation
Documentation makes automation run faster
Because the person who understands it today may be gone in six months, and the next person still has to maintain or extend it
questions.explain: Chapter 2's maintenance topics -- collisions, recursion, upkeep -- all depend on someone being able to explain what automation is supposed to do.

questions.q: What environment does the guide recommend building this lab's design in?
options: Directly in a production org
A sandbox or Developer Edition org, never against production data
A spreadsheet only, with no Salesforce org involved
It doesn't matter which environment is used
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns against building and testing against production data.

questions.q: In the lightweight mapping notation this lesson teaches, what does a diamond represent?
options: A decision point with labeled paths
A single action
A final outcome only
An unrelated note
questions.explain: Diamonds mark branch points -- in the Mill Creek example, 'Days requested > 5?' and 'Manager approves?' are both diamonds.

questions.q: According to the lesson, where did the specific numbers in Lesson 14's Mill Creek brief (over 5 days, 2 conflicts) most plausibly come from?
options: A random number generator
Salesforce's default approval process settings
Guesswork by the automation builder
A real discovery conversation asking exactly what triggers the problem
questions.explain: HR would not necessarily volunteer those specifics unprompted -- a well-asked discovery question is what produces that precision.
